text:
Recent work favors evidence-level evaluation over textual similarity: a 2025/2026 recommendation study finds high BERTScore can coexist with poor statement-level factuality ([Kabongo & Guigue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24366)). Its review-derived evidence is unavailable here; the transferable method is atomic claims checked against permitted evidence. Proposed probes: record the explicit request, supporting title/description spans, and separate labels for specific intent match, broad topical relation, supported specification conflict, and unknown. Compare specific matches with broadly related alternatives. Mark duplication only with evidence of the same product, edition, or repeated recommendation; textual similarity alone supports a redundancy flag, not confirmed identity. Metadata grounding does not establish the model’s actual causal reasoning.

Annotation reliability needs task-specific validation: JUDGE-BENCH finds substantial variation across tasks and judges ([ACL 2025](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-short.20/)); selective evaluation supports abstention or escalation when confidence is insufficient ([Trust or Escalate, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.18370)). Practical adaptation: independently double-annotate, audit evidence spans, report raw agreement plus chance-corrected agreement, disagreements, and unknown/coverage rates. With five feedback users per category, retain user-level results and show sensitivity to individual users; repeated recommendations are not independent user observations. Treat these findings as exploratory, without claiming population-wide preferences or latent personality traits.

Keep full-catalog feedback probes separate from pinned sampled-candidate HR@10. Sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation ([Krichene & Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)); 2025 research further examines fidelity and exposure-bias sensitivity ([RecSys 2025](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086)). Preserve the host’s macro validation HR@10 selection rule; use grounded probes to diagnose failure mechanisms, without interpreting sampled HR@10 as full-catalog recommendation quality.
